column1: What is the core invariant distinguishing gesture from control in mark-making?
column2: Gesture uses large-muscle movements (shoulder, elbow, wrist) for fluid, fast, expressive strokes; control uses fine-motor finger coordination for precise, slow, deliberate marks. Mastery requires fluidly shifting between both poles.

column1: What is the most common novice mistake in mark-making mechanics?
column2: Drawing exclusively from the fingers, which cramps the hand and produces timid, scratchy lines instead of engaging the full kinetic chain from the body's core outward.

column1: What is 'line weight variation' and what spatial information does it encode?
column2: The practice of thickening lines in shadow regions and thinning them where form turns toward light, encoding three-dimensional spatial information within a single two-dimensional stroke.

column1: How do gestural drawing and contour drawing differ in priority?
column2: Gestural drawing uses rapid, loose, overlapping strokes prioritizing movement, rhythm, and kinetic energy over accuracy. Contour drawing uses deliberate, continuous observation to trace perceived edges and plane transitions.

column1: What is the defining invariant of the sight-size measurement method?
column2: The drawing surface is positioned so the subject and drawing occupy identical scale within the visual field from a fixed station point, creating a one-to-one correspondence (e.g., a 3-inch head is drawn at 3 inches).

column1: What are the three absolute invariants enforced by sight-size measurement protocol?
column2: 1) The station point (artist's eye position) must remain fixed. 2) The drawing surface must stay in a consistent plane parallel to frontal vision (vertical, perpendicular to line of sight). 3) Lighting on subject and surface must remain consistent throughout the session.

column1: Why does even a six-inch shift in station point invalidate sight-size measurements?
column2: Because shifting position alters parallax relationships, corrupting all previously taken proportional and angular measurements.

column1: What is the 'cone of vision' in perspective theory?
column2: A pyramidal volume extending from the viewer's eye point through the picture plane into the scene; light rays from objects within this cone intersect the picture plane to determine the object's drawn position (analogous to camera lens projection).

column1: How does the horizon line determine whether an object's top or bottom plane is visible?
column2: Objects below the horizon line are seen from above (top planes visible, e.g., a tabletop); objects above the horizon line are seen from below (bottom planes revealed, e.g., a chandelier's underside).

column1: What are vanishing points, geometrically speaking?
column2: Locations on (or above/below) the horizon line where parallel lines in the scene converge when projected to infinity onto the two-dimensional picture plane—geometric consequences of projection, not arbitrary choices.

column1: What is the key perceptual error when a novice only draws a form's outline (e.g., a sphere's silhouette)?
column2: They capture only the boundary condition where the form meets the background, missing the tonal/value information needed to convey volumetric presence and the form's relationship to the light source.

column1: What three tonal elements constitute the minimum viable information set for constructing volumetric form?
column2: Core shadow (the transitional zone away from direct light), cast shadow (projected onto surrounding surfaces), and reflected light (bounced ambient light preventing the shadow side from reading as flat black).
